title: Bridge the Gap — Healthy Cities
description: Twenty-six Delhi-NCR schools and ten funded fellows in eight states. What the Bupa Foundation and Niva Bupa paid for, and what it actually built.
deck: A curriculum on land, water and air inside twenty-six Delhi-NCR schools. And ten people chosen from across India, funded and mentored to pilot a climate and health idea of their own.
identity: Swechha is an environmental organisation in Delhi, working since 2000 — air, the Yamuna, schools, journeys and a five-acre farm.
partnership: In partnership with the Bupa Foundation and Niva Bupa Health Insurance

what.head: Two halves, one year
what.lead: Two strands under one grant. A curriculum that ran inside twenty-six schools across Delhi-NCR, and a nationwide fellowship that backed ten people to pilot their own climate and health projects in the places they already work.

rows.p: Land, water and air taught as one subject through a school year — classroom workshops, twenty exposure trips out into the city, and a green action project each school builds and then has to keep running.
Ninety-five people applied for ten funded places. The ten who got them worked on compost, stepwells, mushrooms, Napier grass, riverbank saplings and native plants, each on their own ground.
Ten final reports, thirty-one testimonial videos, three film series, and a set of figures every fellow counted themselves.

fellows.head: The ten
fellows.lead: One cohort, ten projects, eight states. Every one of them filed a report at the end of it, and every one has a page of its own.

statement.line: Twenty-six schools gave it a place in the year.

schools.head: In the schools
schools.lead: Twenty-six schools gave the curriculum a place in their year. This is what that bought.

rows.p: Land, water and air taught together, in the timetable rather than beside it. Over two thousand students sat in the workshops.
Twenty exposure trips took students into the city the curriculum is about, to look at a drain, a landfill and a stretch of river up close.

prose: A school year is the unit that matters here. A single workshop is a morning. A year is long enough for a bed to be dug, planted, watered through a Delhi summer and replanted — and for the students who did it to be the ones explaining it to the next lot.

green.head: What is still in the ground
green.lead: Twenty gardens across twenty-six schools. A bed goes in where a class will keep it alive after we leave.

rows.p: Twenty of them, chosen and built by the students inside their own school gates.
Over three thousand went into the ground across the twenty-six schools.

prose: A plantation drive is a photograph. A garden is a rota. The difference between them is whether anybody is still turning up in June — so the bed sits inside the gate, a class owns it, and a teacher notices when it dies.

voices.head: What people said
voices.lead: Teachers, farmers, students and volunteers, on what a year of this changed and what it did not.

watch.head: Watch it
watch.lead: Thirty-one testimonial videos came back from the schools and the fellows, filmed through the year on the ground where the work happened.

onward.act_note: Bring your school into the next year of this, or back the next cohort of fellows.

voices.quote: Need of the hour and how else students will learn about managing their own waste.

The Varso Jal Sanchay Abhiyan provided meaningful experiential learning for our students by connecting heritage with water conservation. The visit to Valavav stepwell enhanced their understanding of traditional water systems and instilled a sense of responsibility towards protecting such structures. Initiatives like this are crucial for shaping environmentally conscious youth.
I had never really noticed the details of leaves before this workshop. Drawing them helped me slow down and observe things I usually ignore.

Participating in this project and Soil School activities helped me understand the importance of soil and sustainable agriculture. This experience motivated me to stay connected with agriculture and environmental work.
